terms.definition: Groupings with no running back, where the field is filled with wide receivers on obvious passing downs (00 = five receivers).
One running back, no tight ends and four wide receivers (first digit running backs, second digit tight ends).
One running back, one tight end and three wide receivers; the most-used grouping in the modern NFL.
Personnel shorthand where an asterisk after the two digits marks an extra offensive lineman beyond the usual five, replacing a skill player.
One running back, two tight ends and two wide receivers.
One running back, three tight ends and one wide receiver, a heavy grouping.
A nickel variation with two down linemen, four linebackers and five defensive backs.
Two running backs, no tight ends and three wide receivers.
Two running backs (usually a halfback and a fullback), one tight end and two wide receivers.
Two running backs, two tight ends and one wide receiver, used mainly in short yardage and at the goal line.
Two running backs, three tight ends and no wide receivers; a goal-line or jumbo package.
A nickel-type defense with three down linemen, three linebackers and five defensive backs.
A defensive front of three linemen and four linebackers, usually with four defensive backs behind them.
Three running backs, one tight end and one wide receiver.
A nickel base defense with four linemen, two linebackers and five defensive backs.
A defensive front of four down linemen and three linebackers, normally with four defensive backs.
A front of five defensive linemen and two linebackers, devised at Oklahoma in the 1940s and also known as the Oklahoma defense.
A defensive front of five linemen and three linebackers, which appeared in the 1930s as a response to stronger passing attacks.
A goal-line alignment built on six defensive linemen and one linebacker (the 'pinch' front), with four defenders left in the secondary.
A front of six defensive linemen and two linebackers, popular in the 1930s as passing attacks improved.
An early defensive formation with seven linemen, one linebacker and three defensive backs, invented in 1903.
A vertical passing system created by Don Coryell that combines power running with mid-range and deep passing and uses motion.
A pass-heavy, shotgun-based offense that de-emphasizes the run and builds on a small set of quick, medium and screen pass concepts, usually with four or five receivers.
A block made on a defender from an angle, not head-on (often a down block toward the inside).
A no-huddle style with shortened huddles held much closer to the line of scrimmage, associated with the 1988 Cincinnati Bengals.
A play change the quarterback calls at the line of scrimmage after seeing the defense, replacing the play called in the huddle.
A fade thrown behind or to the back shoulder of the receiver, away from the defender, usually against man coverage.
The area behind the line of scrimmage, and the offensive players (quarterback and backs) who line up there.
A solo block by an offensive lineman, squared up to the defender.
The defensive alignment a team uses by default (for example a 4-3 or 3-4 front) before it changes personnel for a particular offensive look.
A team that uses the nickel package (five defensive backs) as its normal base defense instead of a 4-3 or 3-4.
Big on big / back on backer: linemen block the down linemen and the backs block linebackers.
A long, high-arcing deep pass.
A play in which the quarterback fakes a handoff one way and then runs or rolls the other way to pass or run.
A quick screen to an inside or slot receiver who steps forward and moves toward the sideline, with other receivers blocking.
The quarterback's spoken pattern of signals and rhythm that tells the line when the ball will be snapped.
The middle offensive lineman, who snaps the ball to the quarterback and calls blocking assignments for the line.
An out route followed by a fly route.
A short pass to a back or tight end thrown as a last resort in the quarterback's read progression.
Another name for the strong side of the formation, usually the side where the tight end lines up.
A route in which the receiver runs deep, then breaks back toward the sideline at about 45 degrees to catch the ball near the boundary.
A deep route in which the receiver breaks toward the sideline at about 45 degrees toward the corner of the end zone.
A play-calling system in which each digit of a numbered call is a code for one of nine routes for a receiver.
A run where the back steps one way, then takes the handoff the other way, with backside blockers (a guard, sometimes a tackle too) pulling to lead through the hole.
A route (or pair of routes) where a receiver crosses the field, such as a drag or slant.
An intermediate route where the receiver runs upfield about 12 to 15 yards, then turns back toward the quarterback and sits in open space.
A route in which the receiver runs upfield (about 12 to 15 yards) and turns back inside toward the quarterback.
A block that takes a defender down by hitting him below the waist; legal only in limited situations, and the NFL bars it against receivers in several cases.
A pass concept pairing a vertical clear-out route with a deep dig (square-in) behind it.
A deep inside-breaking route in which the receiver breaks across the field at about 90 degrees, 10 to 15 yards downfield.
A defensive package with six defensive backs on the field, used in obvious passing situations; the sixth back is the dime back.
A snap from the center straight to a player other than the quarterback.
A quick handoff to a back attacking straight ahead into the interior of the defense.
Any route combination designed to stress the safety.
West Coast playbook word for a blitz.
A route in which the receiver runs 5 to 8 yards, cuts outside, and then turns vertically upfield.
A play in which the ball reverses direction twice behind the line of scrimmage, usually with two or three handoffs.
A formation with two slot receivers inside two outside receivers (a four-receiver look), as in the air raid and run and shoot.
Two blockers engage one defender together, often before one climbs to the next level.
A formation with two tight ends and two wingbacks in which the snap goes to a quarterback or halfback moderately deep in the backfield.
A shallow crossing route over the middle that starts very short and may drift deeper across the field.
A run disguised as a pass: the quarterback drops back, then hands off to a back or keeps it.
A formation with no running back in the backfield with the quarterback, so every other eligible receiver is split out or on the line.
A play where a receiver motions into the backfield, takes a direct handoff from the quarterback and runs around the opposite end; often confused with a reverse.
A play-calling system that names plays by concept and formation rather than by route numbers, so players learn tasks from their starting alignment.
A flexible letter for the fourth skill player: the fullback in two-back sets, or the second tight end in one-back sets with two tight ends.
A vertical route down the sideline in which the receiver tries to get on top of the defender, often with a ball thrown to the outside or back shoulder.
A wide receiver who lines up off the line of scrimmage outside another receiver; the term is largely replaced by Z receiver.
A short route to the sideline within a few yards of the line, usually run by a back (or a slot receiver or tight end from inside the numbers).
A trick play: a back takes a handoff, tosses it back to the quarterback, who then throws downfield.
A three-back option formation with a fullback behind the quarterback and two slotbacks near the ends of the line, used mainly by service academies.
The way the offense or defense lines its players up before the snap.

terms.term: Formation tags (Yo, Yoyo, Nasty, Nastier, Book, Open)
terms.definition: Short words at the end of a formation call that set receiver splits: Yo = the Y end takes a five-yard split, Yoyo = Y splits out wide, Nasty = the weak-side X takes a five-yard split, Nastier = both ends take five-yard splits, Book = all receivers inside the numbers, Open = widest receivers halfway between numbers and sideline.
A back or tight end who runs a route right off the snap with no blocking responsibility.
A back who lines up behind the quarterback, typically ahead of the tailback, and mainly blocks, with some carries and catches.
A trick play in which the quarterback deliberately places the ball on the ground so another player, usually a lineman, picks it up and advances it.
A run play with the frontside guard pulling and trapping or leading through the hole.
A pass protection in which linemen step away from the call toward the back side and protect the gap there.
The quarterback's decision on a read option: hand the ball off (give) or pull it and run (keep), based on how the read defender reacts.
A deep route in which the receiver runs straight down the field as fast and deep as he can.
An offensive lineman who lines up on either side of the center, between the center and the tackles.
A hybrid between a fullback and a tight end who lines up a few yards behind the line and blocks or catches passes.
The letter for the primary or featured running back (halfback) in a pro-style formation call.
A long desperation pass thrown toward a group of receivers near the end zone, used as a last resort when time is running out.
The ball-carrying running back; also called a tailback, and in some systems the H back.
A trick play in which the halfback can either throw a pass or run with the ball.
Giving the ball directly from one player to another, most commonly the quarterback to a running back.
A strategy where the quarterback uses an irregular, accented snap-count cadence, hoping the defense jumps offside.
A personnel group with extra tight ends or backs (a 'jumbo' set), used to run the ball and drawing a base defense.
A short route (about 5 to 8 yards) in which the receiver stops and turns back toward the quarterback.
A numbering of the gaps along the line for run calls, with even numbers to the right and odd to the left.
A trick play in which one receiver runs a hook route, catches the ball and laterals it to a teammate.
A receiver or back who takes a quick pass when his assigned defender blitzes (the quarterback's hot read).
A route change by a receiver or back, made when the quarterback sees a blitz, so the ball comes out quickly.
A meeting of two or more players on the field, instead of taking their positions for the snap, to receive instructions for the next play.
An offensive style that avoids delay between plays, often with no huddle, to run many plays quickly and limit defensive substitutions and adjustments.
The word shouted by the quarterback as part of the snap count; it replaced 'hike' in the second half of the 20th century.
A formation with the fullback and the tailback in a line directly behind a quarterback who is under center, the fullback in front.
A snap taken by the quarterback, who then hands or passes the ball on; opposite of a direct snap to another ball carrier.
A zone run aimed inside the tackles; more of a downhill play than outside zone.
The center and the two guards.
A wide receiver screen where the linemen sprint out in front of the receiver as blockers.
A shallow crossing route with a stutter step.
A short-yardage or goal-line package that adds extra tight ends and backs (or other big bodies) in place of receivers.
The Buffalo Bills' full-time hurry-up, no-huddle offense of the early 1990s, named for tight end Keith McKeller.
A 45-degree slide step offensive tackles use off the snap in pass protection.
A pass thrown sideways or backward; teams may lateral any number of times.
A formation devised by Tiger Ellison that overloaded one side of the offensive line for a scrambling quarterback; a forerunner of the run and shoot.
A run-blocking approach where blockers are paired with defenders by rules to create a running lane.
An I formation with three running backs lined up in a straight line behind the quarterback.
A pass play where the tight end and both backs stay in to block instead of running routes, giving the quarterback extra time but only two receivers.
A pass concept in which two receivers run shallow crossing routes close to each other, creating a pick-like traffic problem for man defenders.
The point in an option play where the quarterback and dive back hold the ball together while the quarterback decides whether to give or keep.
A screen where the receiver continues up the middle of the field (similar to a bubble screen).
Movement of one eligible player before the snap, as a lone player moving parallel to or away from the line (NFL: from the backfield; NCAA: one back not moving toward the opponent's goal line).
Motion calls built from a letter plus a spot number (Fox for the F back, Hound for the H back, and a Z version) that send that player in motion to a named location.
A call placed at the front of the play that sends a receiver, usually the Z, by motion into a named formation.
A bootleg where the quarterback has no blockers: he fakes a handoff and runs the other way to pass or run.
A receiver alignment much tighter to the formation than normal, such as a very small gap between the wide receiver and the tight end or tackle.
A defensive package that puts five defensive backs on the field, the extra one being the nickelback, usually in place of a linebacker.
An offense that lines up and runs the next play without first huddling, to save time or keep the defense from substituting.
Receivers numbered from the outside in, with the widest receiver as number one and the next one in as number two.
The five blockers in the middle of the offense: left tackle, left guard, center, right guard and right tackle.
An I formation in which the fullback lines up to one side of the line between the quarterback and the halfback.
The weak side of the formation, away from the tight end.
A route in which the receiver chooses his path after the snap by reading the defender's leverage.
A play in which the ball carrier is chosen after the snap by reading a defender, the quarterback choosing to hand off, keep or pitch.
A route that breaks hard toward the sideline after a vertical stem (about 10 to 15 yards, depending on the author).
A zone run that stretches the defense laterally toward the edge, also called a stretch play, with the lanes read by the runner.
A block that hits the defender so hard he is driven to the ground.

A two-digit shorthand for the offense's skill players on the field: the first digit is the number of running backs and the second is the number of tight ends, with the rest of the five eligible spots being wide receivers.
A nickname for a low (cut) block used in pass protection.
An outside-zone technique where linemen pin a backside defender while the next backside lineman pulls around toward the second level.
A short-shotgun formation: the quarterback lines up a few yards behind the center and the running back sits directly behind him.
A toss from the quarterback to a trailing running back, as on an option play.
A route where the receiver cuts, pivots and turns back the other way (the 'zig' or 'shark' route, similar to an out).
A fake handoff to the running back before the quarterback passes, to draw defenders toward the run.
A play-action protection series where a back fakes into a gap while the other back and the line protect (H2/F2/F3 name which back fakes and which gap).
Playside is the side a play is designed to go toward; backside is the opposite side.
Pass blocking by the line, tight ends and backs that keeps rushers out of the pocket so the quarterback has time and space to throw.
The area behind the line between the two offensive tackles where the blockers shield the quarterback during a pass play.
A deep route in which the receiver runs up the field and breaks at about 45 degrees toward the goalposts in the middle of the field.
A double move combining a post and a corner: the receiver fakes the post and then breaks to the corner.
A gap run featuring a single pulling offensive lineman from the backside of the play.
A formation with two running backs side by side two to three yards behind the quarterback.
The order in which the quarterback checks his receivers on a pass play.
A block by an offensive lineman who steps back out of the line and runs along it to block a defender, usually on a trap or sweep.
A feint of a throw by the quarterback who keeps the ball, trying to fool the defense.
A defensive package of three linemen, one linebacker and seven defensive backs.
The offensive player who takes the snap from the center and hands off, passes or runs the ball; the leader of the offense.
A short-yardage play in which the quarterback takes the snap and immediately runs forward behind or beside the center.
Short, fast-developing throws such as slants and hitches released on one-, two- or three-step drops.
A coaching image for zone blocking: picture a railroad track parallel to the running back's path.
A lineman makes contact and gets outside leverage to seal the defender inside.
The defender (often the end, or a linebacker/safety in an RPO) whose movement tells the quarterback whether to hand off, keep, pitch or throw.
An option run where the quarterback reads a defender (the end on the side of the play) and either hands off or pulls the ball and runs.
A route that changes depending on how the defender plays it (an option route).
A play where a back carries toward one side, then hands or tosses to a teammate (usually a wide receiver) running the opposite way.
A numbering system that organizes a team's pass routes (for example flat 1, slant 2, comeback 3, curl 4, out 5, dig 6, corner 7, post 8, fade 9), also drawn as one diagram.
An offense that emphasizes receiver motion, splits receivers out, and has them choose routes by reading the defenders instead of following a fixed plan.
A play in which the quarterback chooses to run or pass after the snap based on a read.
An offensive player in the backfield who carries the ball, catches passes and blocks; the term covers halfbacks, tailbacks and fullbacks.
A screen to a running back in the flat, built to let pass rushers through before the back catches the ball behind blockers.
Using simple plays that keep the game clock running (including quarterback kneels) late in a game, usually by the leading team, to end the game sooner and deny the opponent possessions.
A three-level passing concept that overloads one side of the defense with a deep, an intermediate and a short route.
A protection call that releases a back to run a route right off the snap with no blocking duty.
A quarterback running out of the pocket on a called pass play to avoid a sack, buy time or gain yards.
A short forward pass to a receiver, usually a running back, who has blockers set up in front of him.
A pre-planned list of opening plays (Bill Walsh scripted about the first 15) practised in advance.
A vertical route run up the middle of the field, between the areas covered by two defenders, to exploit the open space.
The area behind the defensive line where the linebackers play; blockers climb to it.
A number that names a West Coast pass-protection series; the 100 series is the three-step drop.
The requirement that all offensive players be motionless in position for at least one second before the snap (and after any shift).
A short crossing route that stays within a few yards of the line of scrimmage and runs across the formation under deeper routes.
A simultaneous change of position or stance by two or more offensive players after the ball is ready for play and before the snap; all shifting players must then come to a complete stop.
A formation in which the quarterback takes the snap standing several yards behind the center rather than directly behind him.
A short forward pass in which the quarterback palms the ball and shovels it directly forward to the receiver.
An older formation with an unbalanced line, a direct snap to a back deep in the formation, and a wingback.
A shorter, tighter post where the receiver cuts toward the middle at a shallower angle.
An advanced pulling technique that needs difficult footwork.
A pass protection where linemen slide laterally to a called side while the others block the remaining rushers.
A receiver who lines up in the slot, between the split end and the rest of the offensive line, usually a step off the line.
A route in which the receiver runs a slant and then turns upfield on a go; the name is a compression of 'slant and go'.
A pass concept designed to stress the cornerback in Cover 2, built on a short route with a corner route above it.
A run-heavy offensive strategy that relies on a strong running game.
The backward pass from the center that puts the ball in play and starts a scrimmage down.
The signal or cadence the quarterback uses to tell the line when the ball will be snapped, often varied to draw the defense offside.
A short, quick out route in which the receiver breaks toward the sideline right after a short stem.
A receiver who lines up on the line of scrimmage, several yards outside the interior offensive linemen.
A T-formation variant in which the gaps between guards and tackles are about twice as wide as those between the center and guards.
A pass combination of a curl and a flat route, often with a corner route added.
An offense that uses the shotgun and several receivers to spread the defense across the width of the field.
A hard 90-degree break to the sideline from a vertical stem, about 10 to 12 yards deep.
The first part of a route before the break, usually a vertical push that sets up the cut and the defender's leverage.
A short concept where an inside receiver runs about five to six yards and sits down between zone defenders, or breaks away against man; used in the quick game.
A route that fakes a stop (or a hitch or pump) and then continues upfield on a go.
A zone run designed to get the defense moving laterally; the landmark is just inside the last offensive player (outside zone is the same play family).

terms.term: Swap tags (Yax, Zax, Fax, Yaz, Fay, Fez, Change)
terms.definition: Short tags that tell two named players to exchange alignment spots, such as Yax meaning Y and X change places.
A run to the outside with blockers leading the back; sometimes called a power sweep.
A route run by the running back, who swings out of the backfield into the flat.
A concept where the two outside receivers switch places as they run downfield.
A trick variant of the screen pass that involves an offensive tackle as the receiver.
A word or short call added to a play or formation call that modifies it (for example a split, a flip or an added route).
A quick dropback of three steps that gets the ball out fast.
A player who lines up at the end of the offensive line, blocks on runs, and runs pass routes.
A run where the quarterback tosses the ball to a back who curves out toward the sideline.
A New England Erhardt-Perkins call for the double-slant concept.
A letter-system shift that moves the Y to the opposite side while the X and Z adjust their alignments.
A run in which a defender is allowed through the line and then blocked by a pulling lineman, usually a guard coming from the back side.
A block by a pulling lineman, normally a guard, on a defender who was allowed through the line.
An option run with three possible ball carriers: a dive back, the quarterback and a trailing pitch back.
A wide receiver screen thrown to a receiver moving back toward the quarterback, behind blocking receivers.
An alignment with two receivers on the same side of the formation.
A late-half or late-game offense run at speed with a focus on clock stoppage, favoring passes near the sideline and receivers getting out of bounds, to get as many scoring plays as possible.
The quarterback lines up directly behind the center and takes the snap straight from him.
A triple-option run where a dive back attacks inside while the quarterback reads the defensive end and either keeps or pitches.
An offense built on short, high-percentage passes and timing routes (developed by Bill Walsh), with play calls that name the primary receiver's route.
A play-call format in which the call names the formation, then the hole (one of nine numbered gaps) and the blocking scheme and path.
A route that starts toward the sideline, then turns upfield; run by a receiver or running back.
A route that looks like an in-breaking cut or slant, then breaks to the sideline underneath.
A player who lines up wide of the formation and runs routes to catch forward passes.
Offensive linemen spaced wider than normal (about a half to a full yard or more apart) to open passing lanes; the same word also describes where receivers line up (plus, numbers, reduced splits).
A formation in which the ball is snapped directly to a running back (not the quarterback), who can run or pass, with the quarterback often split out as a receiver.
An offense with a wingback, much misdirection running and wishbone-style option concepts.
A back who lines up outside and slightly behind the end of the line, used in single-wing, double-wing and wing-T offenses.
Getting lower than the opponent.
A formation with the quarterback, a fullback behind him and two halfbacks lined up deeper in a Y shape, built for the triple option.
In letter-based systems, the X is the split end: the receiver on the line of scrimmage, usually away from the tight end.
In letter-based play calling, the Y is the tight end (the player who lines up on the end of the line); in some systems it is the offense's third receiver.
A deep two-man crossing combination: one receiver on a deep over route and another on a deep post over the top, often off play-action.
Yards gained by a receiver after the catch.
In letter-based systems, the Z is the flanker: the receiver who lines up a yard off the line of scrimmage, usually to the tight end's side.
A motion call telling the Z to start in the called formation, cross to the offside guard and return to his original spot.
A run-blocking scheme in which linemen block together to create lanes for the runner, with no hole assigned in advance.
A read option run: the line zone-blocks one way while the quarterback reads a defensive end and either hands off or keeps.
A motion call in which the Z starts in the called formation and motions across to the other side.
